title: Degree control and leading products for a bounded ordered monomial basis
statement:
Let $F$ be a field [def-weil-field], and let $A$ be a unital associative $F$-algebra, meaning an $F$-vector space with an associative $F$-bilinear multiplication and an identity $1$. Let $n\geq0$, $q\geq2$ be integers and let $y_1,\ldots,y_n\in A$. For $a=(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ put $y^a=y_1^{a_1}\cdots y_n^{a_n}$ and $|a|=\sum_i a_i$, with empty product $1$. Assume that the $y^a$ with $0\leq a_i<q$ form an $F$-basis of $A$. Put $W=\operatorname{span}_F\{1,y_1,\ldots,y_n\}$ [def-weil-submodule-span] and assume $y_jy_i-y_iy_j\in W$ for all $i,j$ and $y_i^q\in W$ for all $i$. For an integer $d$ let $P_d$ be the span of those bounded basis monomials with $|a|\leq d$, so $P_d=0$ for $d<0$. Every product of $m$ generators $y_i$ lies in $P_m$, and $P_rP_s\subseteq P_{r+s}$ for $r,s\geq0$, where the left side is the span of products. More precisely, for bounded exponent vectors $a,b$ and $m=|a|+|b|$, one has
$$y^ay^b-y^{a+b}\in P_{m-1}\quad\text{if }a_i+b_i<q\text{ for every }i,$$
and
$$y^ay^b\in P_{m-1}\quad\text{if }a_i+b_i\geq q\text{ for some }i.$$
For $n=0$ the assertions include $A=F\cdot1$ and $1\cdot1=1$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36 and its degree/inversion reordering proof, printed pp.200--204; Theorem 10.40, printed p.207, reducing a pth power to degree one. Agent formulation of the degree-tracking input, assuming the bounded basis; no new PBW independence claim.

proof.text: We use spans in the sense of [def-weil-submodule-span]. Their elements are exactly finite linear combinations of their generators: those combinations form a submodule containing the generators, and every such submodule contains the combinations. Thus each $P_d$ is closed under addition, subtraction and scalar multiplication, and $P_d\subseteq P_e$ for $d\le e$, by inclusion of the generating sets. The empty word evaluates to $1=y^0\in P_0$, and $P_{-1}=0$. We prove by strong induction on word length $m$ that every word of length $m$ evaluates into $P_m$; at the same induction stage we prove that its value differs from its nondecreasing rearrangement by an element of $P_{m-1}$. At $m=0$ the rearrangement is the same empty word, so both claims hold.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.200--202 (degree, inversions, adjacent reductions and spanning); Theorem 10.40, printed p.207 (power relation). Elementary degree-tracking adaptation with bounded basis assumed.

proof.text: Fix $m>0$ and assume the degree claim for every length $t<m$. For a word $w=(i_1,\ldots,i_m)$ put $I(w)=\#\{(h,k):h<k,\ i_h>i_k\}$. If $w$ is not nondecreasing, it has adjacent letters $j>i$: otherwise transitivity of all adjacent inequalities would make it nondecreasing. Swap these letters to get $w'$. For any position outside the two letters the total number of its inversions with that pair is unchanged, since the pair has the same two labels before and after the swap. The inversion between the pair disappears. Hence $I(w')=I(w)-1$, while every label multiplicity is unchanged.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.200--202 (degree, inversions, adjacent reductions and spanning); Theorem 10.40, printed p.207 (power relation). Elementary degree-tracking adaptation with bounded basis assumed.

proof.text: Write the word with the adjacent inverted pair as $u(j,i)v$, with context lengths $a,b$, so $a+b=m-2$. Its evaluation minus that of $u(i,j)v$ is $\operatorname{ev}(u)(y_jy_i-y_iy_j)\operatorname{ev}(v)$. The commutator hypothesis and Step 1 express this as a finite linear combination of context words of lengths $a+b=m-2$ or $a+b+1=m-1$. By the outer induction hypothesis these belong to $P_{m-2}$ or $P_{m-1}$, hence their sum belongs to $P_{m-1}$. Induction on $I(w)$ now gives $\operatorname{ev}(w)-y^c\in P_{m-1}$, where $c_i$ counts the occurrences of $i$. Indeed at inversion zero the word already equals $y^c$; otherwise add the swap difference just computed to the induction assertion for $w'$, whose sorted word has the same multiplicities. This proves the rearrangement claim using only smaller lengths, before proving the degree claim at length $m$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.200--202 (degree, inversions, adjacent reductions and spanning); Theorem 10.40, printed p.207 (power relation). Elementary degree-tracking adaptation with bounded basis assumed.

proof.text: The sorted word $y^c$ has $\sum_i c_i=m$. If every $c_i<q$, it is a defining generator of $P_m$. Otherwise choose $i$ with $c_i\ge q$ and factor its consecutive $q$ copies as $y^c=\operatorname{ev}(u)y_i^q\operatorname{ev}(v)$, where the contexts together have length $m-q$. Expanding $y_i^q\in W$ gives a linear combination of words of lengths $m-q$ or $m-q+1$. Because $q\ge2$, both lengths are at most $m-1$; the outer induction hypothesis and monotonicity put their values in $P_{m-1}$. Thus in either case $y^c\in P_m$. Add the rearrangement error from Step 3, which lies in $P_{m-1}\subseteq P_m$. This proves the degree claim for length $m$ and completes the outer induction. The same calculation proves the stronger conclusion $\operatorname{ev}(w)\in P_{m-1}$ whenever some multiplicity of $w$ is at least $q$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.200--202 (degree, inversions, adjacent reductions and spanning); Theorem 10.40, printed p.207 (power relation). Elementary degree-tracking adaptation with bounded basis assumed.

proof.text: Apply the established rearrangement assertion to the concatenation of the ordered words for $y^a$ and $y^b$, of length $m=|a|+|b|$. Its multiplicity vector is $a+b$. If $a+b$ is bounded, its sorted value is exactly the ordered product $y^{a+b}$, so $y^ay^b-y^{a+b}\in P_{m-1}$. If it is not bounded, the last assertion of Step 4 gives $y^ay^b\in P_{m-1}$. At $m=0$ both vectors are zero, only the bounded case occurs, and its difference is $1\cdot1-1=0\in P_{-1}$. No commutativity of $A$ is used: every sorting error was evaluated in its original left and right contexts.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.200--202 (degree, inversions, adjacent reductions and spanning); Theorem 10.40, printed p.207 (power relation). Elementary degree-tracking adaptation with bounded basis assumed.

proof.text: For $r,s\ge0$, expand $x\in P_r$ and $z\in P_s$ as finite sums $x=\sum_a\alpha_a y^a$ and $z=\sum_b\beta_b y^b$ with bounded exponents and $|a|\le r$, $|b|\le s$. Bilinearity gives $xz=\sum_{a,b}(\alpha_a\beta_b)y^ay^b$. Each summand's word has length $|a|+|b|\le r+s$, so Step 4 and monotonicity put it in $P_{r+s}$. Closure under finite linear combinations gives $xz\in P_{r+s}$; taking the span of all such products proves $P_rP_s\subseteq P_{r+s}$. This also covers $r=0$ or $s=0$.

source.place: Theorem 10.36, printed pp.200--202 (degree, inversions, adjacent reductions and spanning); Theorem 10.40, printed p.207 (power relation). Elementary degree-tracking adaptation with bounded basis assumed.

proof.text: If $n=0$, there is exactly one bounded exponent vector, the empty vector, whose monomial is $1$. The assumed basis therefore says that every element of $A$ is a scalar multiple of $1$, so $A=F\cdot1$. There are no positive-length generator words. The only pair of bounded monomials is $1,1$, with product $1\cdot1=1$ by the unital-algebra hypothesis. Thus the preceding conclusions include all the asserted empty-family cases.
